messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marcus is a 42-year-old ship captain who has spent two decades navigating the Atlantic, a career that once gave him a profound sense of mastery and control. That changed eighteen months ago, when his cargo vessel was caught in a coordinated pirate attack off the coast of West Africa. He remembers the sequence with unbearable clarity: the warning shots fired across his bow, the explosion that tore through the engine room, and then the boarding—masked men in military-style uniforms throwing crew members to the deck, screaming orders in a language he couldn't understand. He watched a first mate take a rifle butt to the skull for hesitating. By the time naval forces arrived, three of his men were dead. Marcus was praised for his composure during the crisis, but privately, he had already begun to unravel.

In the months that followed, Marcus found himself unable to shake the certainty that the people responsible had faced no consequences—the attackers had melted back into the coastal chaos, untouchable, unpunished. This belief that justice had failed hardened into something darker: a conviction that he could not rely on anyone else to keep him or his crew safe. He started to see threats everywhere. A delivery truck backfiring on the dock sent him diving for cover. When a deckhand playfully tossed a coil of rope across the hold, Marcus felt his chest seize with the old terror of objects being thrown. He began scanning every face on the pier for signs of danger, reading aggressive intent into ordinary gestures. The world had become a place where violence could erupt without warning, and he was certain that if he let his guard down for even a moment, he would be caught unprepared again.

This hypervigilance toward people became exhausting, but Marcus could not stop. He started choosing his seat in restaurants and at the union hall based on how safe it felt—always with his back to a wall, always facing the door, always calculating escape routes. At home, he struggled to fall asleep because he needed to stay alert, listening for sounds that shouldn't be there. His wife found him pacing the bedroom at 3 a.m., insisting he'd heard something outside. His vigilance also fed his sense of isolation: the more he scanned for threats, the more convinced he became that he was the only one paying attention, the only one who understood how dangerous people really were. Every near-miss, every unexplained sound, every uniformed figure in his peripheral vision seemed to confirm that his distrust was justified.

To manage this overwhelming sense of danger, Marcus developed strategies that only deepened his problems. He began avoiding unfamiliar places entirely, sticking to routes and ports he knew well, refusing charters that would take him into new waters where he couldn't assess the risks. At work, he started dropping important responsibilities—delegating safety inspections to his second mate, skipping the captain's mandatory log reviews, canceling crew meetings because being in a room full of people felt too exposed. When he wasn't working, he turned to gambling, spending long nights at offshore poker tables where the noise and distraction let him forget the memories for a few hours. But each loss at the table, each responsibility he abandoned, only reinforced his belief that he was falling apart, that he couldn't handle his own life. He would think: *If I think about what happened, I'll never get through the day.* So he pushed the memories down, and they came back harder.

The cycle tightened over the months. His avoidance of unfamiliar places meant he turned down a promotion that would have required him to oversee a new shipping route. His wife stopped inviting him to social events because he would either cancel last minute or sit in silence, watching the exits. She told him he wasn't the same man she married—and she was right. Marcus knew he was losing his grip, but he could not see a way out. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment on the bridge last week, when a faulty pressure valve released a loud bang that sounded exactly like the explosion he remembered. He dropped to his knees, shaking, in front of his entire crew. The humiliation was absolute, but it was also the first time he admitted to himself that he could not keep living this way. He is afraid of what therapy will unearth—convinced, in fact, that talking about the event will break him completely. But he is also terrified of what he will become if he does not try.
